title: The Sari - Krishna Gimme the Sari!
summary: During the sacred festival of Gokulashtami, the wandering drama troupe of a neighboring town enacted the famous episode of Krishna Leela ...
keywords: the sari - krishna gimme the sari!
full_text:
During the sacred festival of Gokulashtami, the wandering drama troupe of a neighboring town enacted the famous episode of Krishna Leela upon an open-air wooden stage in the temple square. Guru Paramartha and his five disciples sat in the front row, watching with wide, rapturous eyes.

The actors depicted the famous scene of the celestial cowherd playfully carrying away the colorful saris of the bathing maidens, climbing a kadamba tree, while the maidens pleaded from the water: 'O Krishna, give us back our saris!'

The performance moved the Guru's disciples to their very souls. As they walked back to their ashram under the starry sky, Mudan was so entranced by the drama that his mind became thoroughly unhinged.

'Did you behold the divine beauty of that scene, brothers?' sighed Mudan. 'The Lord perched upon the tree, and the colorful silk garments fluttering like rainbows! I feel the divine spirit of the cowherd stirring within my chest!'

Next morning, the local washerman had spread dozens of brightly colored, freshly washed, and ironed silk saris belonging to the village ladies upon the clean grassy bank of the river to dry in the warm sun. Crimson, emerald, saffron, and indigo silks gleamed across the meadows.

Mudan, walking down to the river to perform his ablutions, saw the sea of colored saris. The drama from the previous night ignited in his foolish brain.

'The hour of divine recreation has arrived!' shouted Mudan.

Gathering up twenty of the finest silk saris in his arms, the stubborn fool scrambled up a tall tamarind tree overlooking the river path. He draped the bright red, green, and golden saris across the boughs, sat cross-legged on a high branch, and began playing an imaginary flute on his fingers!

Presently, the village women arrived at the bank to collect their dry laundry. Finding the grass empty and looking up into the tree, they saw the Guru's disciple perched among the monkeys, draped in their silk garments!

'Hey, Mudan!' shouted the village elder's wife. 'What are you doing up there with our saris? Come down this instant and return our clothes!'

Mudan closed his eyes, swayed his head in divine ecstasy, and sang out in a high, squeaky falsetto: 'Pleaded with tears, fair maidens of Braja! Cry out: "O Krishna, give us our saris!" and perhaps the Lord will grant your prayers!'

The village women stared in disbelief, then exploded in fury. They did not recite devotional poetry; instead, they armed themselves with heavy wooden washing mallets, river stones, and wet clumps of clay!

'We will give you Krishna Leela, you impudent monkey!' shouted the women.

A barrage of stones, clay balls, and heavy mallets rained upon the tamarind tree. Mudan dodged and shrieked as a heavy mallet struck his shin and a wet clay ball hit him squarely in the ear.

Losing his balance, the 'celestial cowherd' tumbled out of the tree, falling into a dense patch of stinging nettles beneath the bank!

The angry women gave him a sound thrashing with their broom handles, retrieved their silks, and marched him in disgrace to Guru Paramartha's ashram.

The village elder's wife reprimanded the Guru: 'Control your mad disciple, O wise Master, before the village council drives you all out of the district!'

When the women departed, Guru Paramartha looked down upon the swollen, nettle-stung Mudan and delivered his judgment: 'Mudan, you were guilty of an unpardonable anachronism! The Kadamba tree of the sacred scripture was an evergreen, while you climbed a tamarind tree! The sacred Leela cannot be performed among tamarind pods!'

Applying soothing sandalwood paste to his stings, Mudan groaned in agreement, having learned that mythology and laundry banks do not mix.
moral: Religious zeal divorced from common sense and propriety leads to utter public embarrassment.
